drafts.title: I ran 100 viral tweets through an AI roaster — 73% had the exact same flaw
drafts.text:
I've been trying to understand what actually makes tweets go viral vs. what makes them good. So I collected 100 tweets with 10k+ likes and ran each one through an AI tweet roaster.

The result surprised me: nearly three-quarters got flagged for the same core issue — statements framed as profound insight that are actually designed to generate reflexive agreement, not genuine thought.

The AI called it 'engagement bait dressed as wisdom.'

I wrote up all 5 patterns it found, with real examples and what good tweets look like instead:
https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/tweet-roaster/blog/i-made-ai-roast-100-viral-tweets-number-one-mistake-appeared-73-percent-2026/

TLDR: virality measures frictionlessness, not quality. They're different things, and most Twitter growth gurus conflate them.

Unpopular opinion: most viral tweets are bad writing.

I ran 100 tweets with 10,000+ likes through an AI roaster. 73% had the same flaw: they make statements vague enough that anyone can project their own experience onto them.

That's not insight. That's a Rorschach test.

Virality maximizes spread. Spread favors frictionlessness. Frictionlessness favors vagueness. And vagueness is the enemy of useful thinking.

The tweets the AI actually respected — specific, falsifiable, information-dense — got a fraction of the engagement.

Choose what you're optimizing for. Just don't confuse the two.

Title: I roasted 20 SaaS landing pages with AI and 18 had the exact same hero section mistake

Body: Spent a Saturday running 20 landing pages through an AI roaster (mix of YC-backed, indie, and funded startups). The AI kept flagging the same thing: hero headlines describing the product instead of the outcome. "AI-powered CRM with workflows" instead of "stop losing sales to slow follow-up." I call it feature theater. The 2 pages that nailed it? Both founders had done customer interviews and rewritten their headline based on what customers actually said. Full breakdown of 6 patterns + before/after rewrites: https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/roast-my-landing-page/blog/i-made-ai-roast-20-saas-landing-pages-same-mistake-18-of-them-2026/

Unpopular opinion: most SaaS landing pages are secretly written for the founder, not the customer.

I ran 20 pages through an AI roaster. 18 had the same problem: the hero described what the product does, not what life looks like after you use it.

One page had 500+ paying customers. Zero social proof above the fold.

Another raised $4M last March. Their hero headline could have been written by a committee who had never met a customer.

The 2 pages that nailed it? Both founders rewrote their headline after talking to real users.

That's the whole secret. The AI just makes it visible.
